title: University of Melbourne Tiegs Museum: pre-register teaching collection, 1893 specimen register, surviving slide collection and modern re-addressing

principal_upgrade.previous_state: The Tiegs Museum was an A+ comparator because an extensive historical microscope-slide collection and Spencer-related material were known to survive, but nineteenth-century item-level addressing had not been reconstructed.
principal_upgrade.new_state: University historical research identifies the actual departmental Register of Specimens, begun in 1893, and shows how a teaching collection founded in 1887 accumulated for six years before formal cataloguing. Current University documentation independently confirms an extensive microscope-slide collection with Spencer and former-researcher contributions. A current Victorian Collections object demonstrates that old register/batch information can still be translated into a modern MUZD identifier, though the available example is a skeleton rather than a slide.

grade.old_register_to_modern_MUZD_object_readd: S demonstrated on a non-slide object

institutional_architecture.founding_context: Walter Baldwin Spencer specified a Biology building with laboratories, live-animal/dissection space, aquarium and greenhouse. Because National Museum specimens were considered too valuable for student handling, Spencer built a separate teaching collection for actual use.
institutional_architecture.current_slide_endpoint: The University states that the Tiegs Museum retains an extensive microscope-slide collection, including contributions from Walter Baldwin Spencer and other former departmental researchers, and that the museum remains important to undergraduate teaching.

register.title: Register of Specimens in the Museum of the Biological School, University of Melbourne
register.function: Catalogue of most of the museum collection and the principal primary source for the museum's early history.
register.pre_register_gap: The collection began in 1887, but aside from sketchy labels there was no systematic written record for about six years.
register.example_of_retroactive_addressing: A shell collected by Spencer in Queensland in 1892 was entered later as register entry 159; the object therefore existed before its formal catalogue address.
register.first_recorded_entry: Entry 1, Bufo vulgaris, donated by Mr Boulanger / British Museum, 1893.
register.international_batch_example: Prague Museum exchange, 1902, register entries 1208–1217, noted as received named.
register.recording_limit: The historical account repeatedly notes incomplete metadata and later losses/disposals; the register is a powerful address system but was never a complete transparent mirror of the physical collection.

modern_readdressing_demonstration.historical_record_state: Recorded with a batch transferred from the 'Nat. Sc. Dept' in September 1899; Frederick McCoy is entered as identifier. Current catalogue reconstructs the batch as MUZD1113–1126.
modern_readdressing_demonstration.physical_mark: An older accession number '2259' is written on the sternum.
modern_readdressing_demonstration.significance: The object demonstrates how historical register/batch information and an older physical number are carried into the modern MUZD namespace.
modern_readdressing_demonstration.guard: This object is a skeleton, not a microscope slide. It proves the museum's re-addressing practice, not the slide-specific crosswalk.

research_mechanism.chain: working teaching collection before formal catalogue -> 1893 register address -> later transfers/reclassification -> modern MUZD address
research_mechanism.strong_claim: At Melbourne, cataloguing followed collecting. The 1893 register imposed a retrievable institutional address on a teaching collection that had already existed for six years, and modern cataloguing can still preserve or reconstruct older batch and object addresses.
research_mechanism.slide_specific_question: Can one Spencer or other nineteenth-century microscope slide be followed from surviving label -> 1893 register or later departmental register -> current storage/MUZD address?

comparison.Cole: address system designed with the publication from the outset
comparison.Cajal: successive institutional addresses accumulate around the same preparation
comparison.Tiegs: formal institutional address arrives after collection growth and retrospectively orders a pre-existing teaching collection

critical_guards: Do not assume the 1893 specimen register contains every historical microscope slide; the source itself describes incomplete early recordkeeping.
Do not infer that every current Spencer-attributed slide dates to the nineteenth century without maker/date/label evidence.
Do not use the MUZD1116 skeleton as slide provenance; it is a control demonstrating the museum's address translation practice.
Keep collection survival, nineteenth-century subset identification and item-level register crosswalk as separate evidential layers.
next_bounded_actions: Request/export the microscope-slide inventory filtered by creator/contributor Spencer and date before 1900, including label text and current box/tray/storage address.
For two or three nineteenth-century slide candidates, query the 1893 Register and any later departmental slide registers using subject, donor/preparator, locality and old number.
Photograph front/back labels before any broad Melbourne archival search; use those exact terms against the Register and Registrar correspondence.
